## Weak Instruments

The usual normal approximation to the IV estimator may be unreliable when the instrument is weak.
To illustrate this, consider the simple model

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + u_i, \qquad
X_i = \pi_1 Z_i + v_i, \qquad
u_i = v_i + e_i,
$$

where $Z_i$, $v_i$, and $e_i$ are mutually independent $\mathcal N(0,1)$ random variables, and observations are i.i.d. across $i$.
Set $\beta_0=0$ and $\beta_1=2$.
Here $Z_i$ is a valid instrument because $\mathbb E[Z_i u_i]=0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i,X_i)=\pi_1$, whereas $X_i$ is endogenous because $\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,u_i)=1$.

The just-identified IV (2SLS) estimator of the slope is

$$
\hat\beta_{1,\mathrm{IV}}
=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (Z_i-\bar Z)(Y_i-\bar Y)}
       {\sum_{i=1}^n (Z_i-\bar Z)(X_i-\bar X)}.
$$

When $\pi_1$ is fixed and nonzero, conventional asymptotic theory gives

$$
\sqrt n(\hat\beta_{1,\mathrm{IV}}-\beta_1)
\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N\left(0,\frac{2}{\pi_1^2}\right).
$$

Thus, the conventional Gaussian approximation to the distribution of the estimator $\hat\beta_{1,\mathrm{IV}}$ is
$\mathcal N\bigl(2,\,2/(n\pi_1^2)\bigr)$.
We compare that approximation with the simulated sampling distribution for a strong instrument ($\pi_1=0.5$) and a weak instrument ($\pi_1=0.02$).

```{webr}
set.seed(1121)

n <- 2000          # sample size in each replication
B <- 1000          # number of Monte Carlo replications
beta1 <- 2         # true slope
pi_strong <- 0.5   # strong first stage
pi_weak <- 0.02    # weak first stage

iv_strong <- numeric(B)
iv_weak <- numeric(B)

for (b in 1:B) {
  Z <- rnorm(n)
  v <- rnorm(n)
  e <- rnorm(n)
  u <- v + e

  X_strong <- pi_strong * Z + v
  X_weak <- pi_weak * Z + v
  Y_strong <- beta1 * X_strong + u
  Y_weak <- beta1 * X_weak + u

  Zc <- Z - mean(Z)
  iv_strong[b] <- sum(Zc * Y_strong) / sum(Zc * X_strong)
  iv_weak[b] <- sum(Zc * Y_weak) / sum(Zc * X_weak)
}

plot_iv_hist <- function(estimates, pi, label) {
  normal_sd <- sqrt(2 / (n * pi^2))
  half_width <- 5 * normal_sd
  edges <- seq(beta1 - half_width, beta1 + half_width,
               length.out = 41)
  shown <- estimates >= min(edges) & estimates <= max(edges)
  h <- hist(estimates[shown], breaks = edges, plot = FALSE)

  # Normalize by ALL replications, including those outside the plot.
  # Thus the bar heights are comparable with the Gaussian density.
  bar_density <- h$counts / (length(estimates) * (edges[2] - edges[1]))
  ymax <- 1.15 * max(bar_density,
                     dnorm(beta1, mean = beta1, sd = normal_sd))

  plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = range(edges), ylim = c(0, ymax),
       main = paste0(label, " (pi = ", pi, ")"),
       xlab = "IV estimate", ylab = "Density",
       cex.main = 0.95, cex.axis = 0.85, cex.lab = 0.9)
  rect(head(edges, -1), 0, tail(edges, -1), bar_density,
       col = "grey80", border = "white")

  xx <- seq(min(edges), max(edges), length.out = 400)
  lines(xx, dnorm(xx, mean = beta1, sd = normal_sd),
        col = "red", lwd = 2)
  abline(v = beta1)
  mtext(sprintf("%.1f%% outside displayed range", 100 * mean(!shown)),
        side = 3, line = 0.15, cex = 0.7)
}

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 3.5, 3, 1))
plot_iv_hist(iv_strong, pi_strong, label = "Strong")
plot_iv_hist(iv_weak, pi_weak, label = "Weak")
par(old_par)
```

The bars show the Monte Carlo sampling distribution. The red curve is the conventional Gaussian approximation, and the vertical line marks the true value $\beta_1=2$.
The horizontal scales are different in the two panels. In the weak-instrument panel, extremely large or small estimates are omitted from the displayed range; the percentage omitted is reported above the plot. 

With a strong instrument, the Gaussian approximation typically describes the simulated distribution well. With a weak instrument, the finite-sample distribution can be asymmetric and heavy-tailed, so the Gaussian approximation can be misleading.

*Note:* Here $\pi_1=0.02$ is held fixed. Thus, conventional asymptotic normality eventually applies as $n\to\infty$. This simulation illustrates **a poor finite-sample Gaussian approximation**, rather than the nonnormal limit obtained under local-to-zero weak-instrument asymptotics.
